How I Did It: Bug Shooter

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

Centipede showed up in my building in 1980 and never once sat empty. A kid named Denny had his initials welded to the top of that high-score list for the better part of a year — D-E-N, proud as anything. Then one Saturday in '82 a girl named Fran beat his score by about four thousand points and just stood there grinning at him while he checked his pockets for another quarter. That rivalry ran for months and I never had to buy either one of them a soda, they were feeding my machine plenty on their own. Somewhere in there a kid tried to jam a Canadian quarter in the coin slot and I spent twenty minutes with a butter knife getting that machine breathing again.

What the remodel changed

The old version I hacked together myself in '25 had the bug just bouncing along a row and dropping down when it hit a wall — good enough, but it didn't really feel like a chain, more like a train of boxes bumping into each other. This time the crew built it so every segment actually follows the one in front of it, like a real conga line of bugs, and if you shoot it in the middle the whole thing splits into two separate bugs that keep crawling on their own. They also taught it "deltaTime" again — same trick as the tennis game — so everything from the bug's crawl speed to my little mushroom-healing bonus ticks along steady no matter how fast your computer is. And they put in the screen shake and a burst of sparks on every kill, which I did not think I needed until I saw it and then I very much needed it.

The spell that did it

Build our Centipede game against the shared GZ engine. A field of mushrooms that take four hits each. A centipede made of segments that really follow each other like a chain, winding down the screen, reversing at walls and mushrooms. If I shoot a body segment it should turn into a mushroom and split the chain into two independent bugs. Give me a spider that bounces around my zone, a flea that drops in to restock mushrooms when they get thin, and a scorpion that poisons mushrooms so the centipede dives straight down when it touches one. Score by proximity for the spider kill. Three lives, and heal a few mushrooms when I die so it isn't hopeless.

Under the hood

  • Everything runs on a 30-column grid, but the bug's movement and the mushroom-heal timers all tick forward by the real elapsed seconds — no fixed per-frame nudge like my first draft.
  • Each centipede is its own little chain object. When you kill a body segment, I just slice its segment list in two — everything ahead of the hit stays one bug, everything behind it becomes a brand-new bug with its own head. Turns out that's most of the trick right there.
  • The scorpion doesn't hurt the centipede directly — it tags a mushroom as poisoned, and the next segment that runs into that particular mushroom checks the flag and heads straight for the floor instead of turning around.
  • When you lose a life, I go find some of the mushrooms you'd already chipped away at and heal them back a notch, a few points and a little tick sound each, spread out over about a second so it doesn't all clatter at once.
